implementation_notes: In a Spring (or CDI/Quarkus) application the container is the DAO factory: each store's DAO is a bean - a @Repository or a @Bean method constructed with that store's DataSource - and the active store is chosen by profile, property or qualifier, or by injecting a whole Map<String, UserDao>. Constructor injection against the DAO interface replaces both the abstract factory and the store switch, and the JDK's ServiceLoader covers plugin-style stores, which is why this language is classified library rather than manual. Hand-write the classic DAOFactory only in container-free code such as plain JDBC tools, batch jobs or libraries.
pitfalls: Two beans implementing the same DAO interface without a profile or @Primary makes the context fail (or silently pick one); qualify the intended bean explicitly.
A singleton DAO that captures a request- or tenant-scoped DataSource leaks one tenant's connection to everyone; scoped proxies or per-tenant factories are required.
@Profile/@ConditionalOnProperty selection hides configuration mistakes until context refresh; validate store keys and connections at boot instead of on the first request.

variants.name: ServiceLoader-based factory registry
variants.implementation_notes: For plugin-style stores the JDK's ServiceLoader is the registry: declare the DAO factory interface as the service, list implementations in module-info (provides ... with ...) or META-INF/services, and select by a store key exposed on each provider via stream() and filter. A new store JAR is dropped in without recompiling the application, and this is the JDBC driver's own mechanism (java.sql.Driver is a ServiceLoader service), so it fits persistence code naturally. It complements container wiring rather than replacing it, and it is the hand-written factory's best replacement in plain-JDK projects.
pitfalls: ServiceLoader instantiates lazily and caches; reload() is needed to see newly deployed providers, and iteration is not thread-safe without external synchronisation.
Providers need a public no-argument constructor or a static provider() method; factories requiring a DataSource must take configuration in the factory method instead.
Class-path discovery (META-INF/services) and module-path discovery (provides/uses) differ; a provider invisible to the loader fails at runtime with ServiceConfigurationError, not at compile time.

variants.name: Classic abstract DAOFactory (catalog form)
variants.idiom_name: abstract DAOFactory + concrete factories + getDAOFactory(which) selection
variants.implementation_notes: The Core J2EE form, still right for plain-Java code with no container: an abstract DAOFactory declares one creation method per DAO interface, concrete factories (OracleDAOFactory, CloudscapeDAOFactory) implement them against that store's DataSource and SQL dialect, and a static getDAOFactory(which) or registry map returns the concrete factory. The store decision stays in one class, the DAO families are independently testable, and the DAO interfaces are what survives a later move to a container.
pitfalls: A factory that creates its DataSource per call multiplies pools; create the DataSource once and pass it into the factory.
A mutable static selection method (or a lazily cached repository-wide instance) turns the factory into global state that tests cannot isolate.
